impact: The research begins pre-iPhone at UCC in Cork City, Ireland. 1st year undergradate geography undergraduate Seán Lynch is challenged with coming up with a dissertation, pairs a handheld GPS with a digital camera to map litter and empower others in the community to tell their story.

During a Masters in Science in GIS & Remote Sensing, Seán is introduced to OpenStreetMap. Inspired by its open values, he goes looking for its real-time data collection layer which didn't exist. The idea for OpenLitterMap was born later that day.
Lynch completes a second MSc in Geographic Science where he reviewed all the available litter mapping, plastic pollution and citizen science literature which informed the development of OpenLitterMap
OpenLitterMap.com is registered.
OpenLitterMap launches to the public — an open, interactive map of the world's litter.
Seán Lynch shares the OpenLitterMap vision at TEDxTallaght.

The founding peer-reviewed paper is published — Lynch, S. (2018), 'OpenLitterMap.com – Open Data on Plastic Pollution with Blockchain Rewards (Littercoin)', Open Geospatial Data, Software and Standards 3:6.
The platform launches in Spanish — the first of many translations.
OpenLitterMap is featured at State of the Map, the global OpenStreetMap conference.
First application to Ireland's Discover Programme — filed through a company only days old — is ignored.
The native iOS app arrives on the App Store.
The native Android app launches on Google Play.
Mobile App v2 launches with a redesigned tagging experience and a new introduction video.
The project is presented at the European Space Agency's Φ-week Earth-observation summit.
OpenLitterMap v2.0 goes live, a major rebuild of the web platform.
OpenLitterMap v2 becomes fully open source.
Teams launch letting groups map and compete together.
A major upgrade transforms the real-time global map of every recorded piece of litter.
OpenLitterMap is awarded $50,000 by the Cardano community, it's first source of funding
OpenLitterMap is recognised as a Digital Public Good by the UN-endorsed Digital Public Goods Alliance.
highlight: Ireland's only UN Digital Public Good

impact: The Amazon Sustainability Data Initiative (ASDI) features OpenLitterMap for building open citizen-science infrastructure on AWS.
Second application to the Discover Programme — pairing OpenLitterMap with LitterWeek digital-skills training — is rejected.
The UN Statistical Commission endorses the Copenhagen Framework on Citizen Data, recognising citizen-generated data within national data ecosystems.
The OECD publishes 'Embedding Citizen Science into Research Policy' (STI Policy Paper No. 175), setting out ten recommendations for governments.
'The Democracy Gap', a 71-page submission, is hand-delivered to UNESCO and OECD headquarters in Paris.
MAPS — the Mapping Audit of Public Science — begins: a Freedom of Information campaign seeking transparency on national litter data and its public funding.
The Department of Climate, Energy and the Environment refuses the first MAPS request in full; a redesigned request is filed.
LitterWeek.org launches — a five-day digital-skills programme for schools — with its first pilots running in Cork.
OpenLitterMap v5 launches — the biggest rebuild in the project's history: 521,000 photos migrated to a unified tagging system, with a new time-series metrics database powering every stat.
OpenLitterMap clears Level 1 of re-certification under the Digital Public Goods Alliance's updated standard.
An OpenLitterMap TidyTowns webinar draws 130+ registrations across dozens of committees; participating committees begin daily structured collection.
The Taoiseach tells the Dáil that cigarette litter outside State institutions is unacceptable, and orders a re-examination.
Ireland assumes the Presidency of the Council of the European Union for July–December 2026.

Day One of the Presidency: parliamentary questions on citizen science and national litter data are tabled across three Government departments, and The Democracy Gap is formally submitted to the Oireachtas FHERIS Committee.

Among the Day One questions, OpenLitterMap — Ireland's only UN Digital Public Good, in the Taoiseach's own constituency — is named directly. The reply engages none of it: no assessment of the Copenhagen Framework, and none of the OECD's ten recommendations implemented. The first of two unacknowledged namings on the Oireachtas record.
The Department of Enterprise cites LitterWeek as a Case Study for Digital Inclusion.

The remaining Day One questions are answered: the Minister with responsibility for research cannot name a funding instrument under which a citizen-led organisation may apply as lead applicant; the records sought on citizen-science funding and past Discover projects are promised 'in a follow-up communication' — still outstanding; and litter.ie, the national litter-monitoring website for over twenty years, is confirmed decommissioned in June for failing the Government's own publication standards.

A reply on the Taoiseach's cigarette-butt re-examination does not address whether it will weigh citizen-generated evidence such as OpenLitterMap (named a second time). It places €1m of 2026 litter funding on the record — €750k in awareness grants and a €250k fund — with nothing allocated to citizen science.
The Oireachtas FHERIS Committee notes The Democracy Gap correspondence.
Four Freedom of Information requests filed with Research Ireland — covering the 2019 and 2024 Discover applications and the agency's citizen science policy record — are acknowledged the same day.
Fifteen new parliamentary questions across six departments are sent to five supporting TDs.
